name: Three Principles of the People
info: The Three Principles of the People are the nationalist, republican, anti-imperialist ideology of Sun Yat-sen, made of nationalism, democracy and people's welfare; set out in 1905, they became the official ideology of the Kuomintang's state.

facts.thinkers: Sun Yat-sen, who set out the Principles; Hu Hanmin, Wang Jingwei and Feng Ziyou, who fleshed them out in Minbao; Zhu Zhixin, who defended the Tongmenghui's “state socialism”; Chiang Kai-shek, who interpreted them as party leader; Dai Jitao, whose conservative reading the Kuomintang followed; Liang Qichao, the reformist rival whose ideas on the nation and the general will left their mark
facts.texts: the Tongmenghui manifesto (1905); Sun's article in the first issue of Minbao (1905); The International Development of China; The Fundamentals of National Reconstruction (1924); Sun's lectures, published as The Three Principles of the People (English translation by Frank Price, 1927); Sun's political testament (1925, drafted by Wang Jingwei)
facts.ideas: nationalism, with China's revival from imperial domination; democracy, with the four powers of the people (suffrage, recall, initiative, referendum) and a five-branch government; people's livelihood, covering clothing, food, housing and mobility; land equalisation by self-assessment; a distinction between the sovereignty of the people and the ability of the government; political tutelage before constitutional government; the Confucian ideal of Datong
facts.today: the Kuomintang made the Principles the official ideology of its state, and after its government's retreat to Taiwan Chiang Kai-shek added texts on education and leisure; the Chinese Communist Party honours Sun, less so the Principles, and in Deng Xiaoping's era linked his economic plans to the Four Modernisations; Singapore's People's Power Party, founded in 2015, took them as its guiding ideology

t: Sun Yat-sen first set out the Principles of nationalism, democracy and people's welfare in 1905, and the Tongmenghui, formed in Tokyo that year, put them in its manifesto.
Sun's democracy rested on a distinction between the people's sovereignty and the government's ability, a government of five branches and a period of political tutelage before constitutional rule.
After Sun's death in 1925 the Kuomintang made the Principles, as Sun gave them in his 1924 lectures and Chiang Kai-shek interpreted them, the official ideology of its state.
dyk: The name “Three Principles of the People” comes from Feng Ziyou, who later claimed that while editing a Hong Kong Tongmenghui paper he shortened the phrase “promoting nationalism, democracy, and people's welfare” into the term.
ev: Sun Yat-sen founds the radically anti-Qing Revive China Society
Sun first sets out the ideas behind his Principles in a speech in Brussels, and the Tongmenghui is formed in Tokyo
Sun reiterates the idea of a political transition in the Chinese Revolutionary Party, with an indefinite revolutionary period of party rule
Sun dies of liver cancer after signing a testament that urges the Kuomintang to hold fast to the Principles
The Organic Law reorganises the Nationalist government on the principle of political tutelage, with five branches
Sun's Whampoa address, whose opening line invokes the Principles, becomes the Kuomintang's party anthem
Mao Zedong's On New Democracy reads the Principles as the “New Three Principles of the People”
Singapore's People's Power Party is founded with the Principles as its official guiding ideology

sections.origins:
In 1894 Sun Yat-sen founded the radically anti-Qing Revive China Society. After the failure of its 1895 uprising he entered a years-long exile, part of it in England, which he later described as the time when his Principles were conceived. After another uprising in 1900 he had to compete for the support of overseas Chinese with the reformist leaders Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, and he spent much of 1903 to 1905 visiting Chinese communities across the world. The Revive China Society member Liu Cheng-yu later claimed in his memoirs that a conversation with Sun in San Francisco in 1904 inspired him to add the principle of people's livelihood to his platform.

Around the same time Sun's rhetoric took on the anti-Manchuism of the newly forming radical student movements, whom he courted. In a speech in Brussels in 1905 he set forth the ideas behind his Principles for the first time. In October 1905 Sun, Huang Xing, Song Jiaoren and other radicals formed the Tongmenghui in Tokyo, whose manifesto set forth the Principles as part of its programme, and Sun wrote an article explaining them for the first issue of its newspaper Minbao. Younger collaborators, among them Hu Hanmin, Wang Jingwei and Feng Ziyou, then fleshed them out into an ideology.
sections.ideas:
Nationalism was the first principle. Sun held that nations form through five natural forces: blood kinship, common language, common livelihood, common religion and common customs. He asserted five main biological races, white, black, red, brown and yellow, and, influenced by social Darwinism, saw reproduction as a factor in national survival, fearing that China's slower population growth endangered it. He blamed China's misfortunes on the loss of national consciousness, to be revived through the clan loyalties of a people he called a “sheet of loose sand” and through traditional virtues. By the 1920s anti-imperialism had become a mainstay of his nationalism.

In the second principle, democracy, Sun proposed dividing power among five branches, adding oversight and civil service examination, drawn from the traditional censorate and the keju, to the legislative, executive and judicial branches. He distinguished the sovereignty of the people from the ability of the government, which was to be left to experts, and gave the people four powers: suffrage, recall, initiative and referendum. He opposed federalism, favouring county autonomy, and held that individual liberty must be broken down so that the Chinese could be pressed together like sand with cement.

The third principle, people's livelihood, covered clothing, food, housing and mobility. It combined state-led modernisation, with private capital limited but not abolished, and a plan for land equalisation drawing on Henry George. Sun linked it to socialism but doubted Marxism's methods for China, and held that cooperation, not class struggle, drove history.
sections.spread:
From 1905 to 1907 Sun and, to a much greater degree, collaborators such as Wang Jingwei, Hu Hanmin and Song Jiaoren wrote articles on the Principles in Minbao to define them as an ideology and to fight the Tongmenghui's reformist foes, among them Liang Qichao. Anti-Manchuism was one theme: Wang Jingwei argued in A Nation of Citizens that Manchu racial incompatibility made constitutionalism a ploy to strengthen Manchu power. The Tongmenghui also prescribed a three-stage transition from imperial rule to democracy. Sun restated it in 1914 as a single revolutionary period of party rule and in 1924 as military rule, political tutelage and constitutional government.

In 1924 Sun gave a series of lectures on the Principles to Kuomintang cadres, six each on nationalism and democracy and four on livelihood. Chen Jiongming's attack of 1922 had destroyed Sun's notes for a written text, and the lectures were transcribed and revised under his direction by Huang Changgu and Zou Lu. After the Kuomintang's victory in the Northern Expedition the text was granted canonical status as the definitive exposition of his thought. Frank Price made an English translation in 1927, and after the government's retreat to Taiwan Chiang Kai-shek completed the discussion of livelihood with texts on education and leisure.
sections.power:
After Sun's death Chiang Kai-shek rose to become the Kuomintang's most important figure. From May 1926 to June 1928 he commanded the Northern Expedition, which united much of the country, formed the National Government and purged the Chinese Communist Party from the Kuomintang. From 1928 to 1949 the Kuomintang ruled as the government of mainland China. Under the 1928 Organic Law the government was reorganised according to Sun's principle of political tutelage, with party organs in supreme command over every aspect of government, and it consisted of the five branches Sun had described: the Executive, Legislative, Judicial, Control and Examination Yuan.

Under Kuomintang rule the Principles were raised to the status of political dogma. Influenced by Dai Jitao's conservative interpretations, the party read them in continuity with Confucian virtues, which Chiang's New Life Movement also stressed. They became part of official ritual: every Monday members of public institutions gathered to bow to Sun's portrait and hear readings of his Testament. The Principles were inscribed on Sun's tomb, and his Whampoa address, whose opening line invokes them, became the party anthem in 1930 and the national anthem in 1937. Under Kuomintang rule Sun's thought achieved canonical status as part of an overall cult of personality.
sections.critiques:
The Principles were argued over from the start. In Minbao, Sun's allies answered Liang Qichao, who held that China was unready for a republic and that founding one meant revolution and chaos, and who wanted the dynasty turned into an enlightened autocracy. Sun's side replied that republicanism was the most modern and therefore the best form of government and was rooted in Chinese culture. Liang also held that social revolution was unnecessary and possibly harmful and that China needed a programme of capitalist industrial benefit; Zhu Zhixin answered that the Tongmenghui's socialism meant a “state socialism” aimed only at monopolies, and Feng Ziyou that social revolution would spare China the inequality of the West.

Within the movement there were disagreements as well. Sun at first did not share the harshly anti-Manchu racism of radicals such as Zhang Binglin and Zou Rong; Zhang was willing to trade territory for a homogeneous Han state, which Sun refused, rejecting the expulsion or mass murder of the Manchu minority. Sun criticised the May Fourth students' demands for greater individual liberty, and his opposition to federalism brought him into conflict with his former ally Chen Jiongming. After 1911 the Kuomintang under Song Jiaoren made socialism a programme of industrial development, which dismayed Sun's Guangdong followers led by Hu Hanmin. The framing of democracy in the Principles differs from the typical Western view, resting on Liang's interpretation of the general will, which puts the power of the group above individual freedoms.
sections.legacy:
In the Communist Party's own history, Mao Zedong's party reached an agreement with the Kuomintang after years of civil war and Japanese aggression to cooperate on the basis of Sun's Principles, which became known as the Second United Front. In On New Democracy (1940) Mao held that the Principles should be understood as the “New Three Principles of the People”, embodied in the Three Great Policies of alliance with Russia, cooperation with the Communist Party and assistance to peasants and workers. After the People's Republic came to power Sun continued to receive honour, but less of it, and less for the Principles than for the Three Great Policies. After the rise of Deng Xiaoping he was hailed for his plans of economic development, which were connected to Deng's Four Modernisations.

Abroad, the Vietnam Revolutionary League, a union of nationalist groups run by the Việt Nam Quốc Dân Đảng, drew inspiration from the Principles in opposing Japanese and French imperialism, and the motto Independence, Freedom, Happiness of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam was also taken from them. The Khamba leader Pandatsang Rapga adopted them for his Tibet Improvement Party and translated them into Tibetan. In Singapore the People's Power Party, founded in 2015, took them and the five branches of government as its guiding ideology.

summary: The Three Principles of the People, nationalism, democracy and people's welfare, are the ideology Sun Yat-sen set out in 1905 and expounded in his 1924 lectures. The Kuomintang made them the official ideology of its state, and they left marks on the Communist Party's thought and on movements in Vietnam, Tibet and Singapore.
references: Sun Yat-sen, translated by Pasquale d'Elia, The Triple Demism of Sun Yat-Sen (AMS Press, 1974)
notes: Start 1905, circa false: the article says Sun first set forth the Principles in 1905 (Brussels speech, Tongmenghui manifesto, Minbao article). End null: the article reports a party founded on the Principles in 2015.

The article contradicts itself on the year of Sun's lectures: its introduction says January to August 1924, its section on the lectures says 1921 (while the Kuomintang held its 1st National Congress). The text says 1924 in the lectures' title only where the article does (the 'Whampoa' and 'Fundamentals' dates are separate); the editor should decide. The 1924 lectures are also said to have been delivered at that Congress.

The article's Origins paragraph about the Tongmenghui manifesto and Minbao is repeated and broken ('whose party manifesto set forth the Three Principles ( whose party manifesto...'); I used only the clear parts.
Liu Cheng-yu's San Francisco story and Feng Ziyou's coining of the term are each the person's own later claim in the article, and are attributed so.
The lead's 'cult of personality' sentence is the article's own; I used it only in the power section, as the article states it.

Left out: the legend of Sun's tomb and the Mandate of Heaven; See also items (Chiangism, Dai Jitao Thought, Unidemism); the Zhonghua minzu and wuzu gonghe discussion; the Datong passage. The article gives no figures for repression; the only repression it names is the purge of the Chinese Communist Party from the Kuomintang in the Northern Expedition.
Sun's lecture count: 16 given (six, six, four); the article says two more were intended but not given.
